comparator.name: Human Geography and Planning
comparator.sourceNotes: The regular programme has 60 EC each year. Healthy Ageing is the first of four options for the 5 EC restricted elective. The 30 EC of third-year choice remains open. The 5 and 10 EC parts of the Bachelor’s Project form one 15 EC thesis.
components: Reflecting on Human Geography and Planning
Geography, Planning and the European Union

alternatives.label: Human geography, planning and sustainability
alternatives.concept: Studies how communities, institutions and environmental change shape places. Courses in spatial planning, Earth observation and water management combine with sociology, policy and research methods.
alternatives.labelReason: Introductory sustainability and economics and a supported regional project precede geospatial planning, Earth observation, water adaptation and advanced analysis. Earth Observation and Spatial Planning draw on the two sustainability gateways.
progression: Introductory sustainability and economics and a supported regional project precede geospatial planning, Earth observation, water adaptation and advanced analysis. Earth Observation and Spatial Planning draw on the two sustainability gateways.

alternatives.label: Governance, public policy and environmental justice
alternatives.concept: Studies how institutions make decisions and how those decisions affect communities. Public economics, law and policy analysis support questions about inequality, property and environmental justice.
alternatives.labelReason: Sociology, law and economics support later study of constitutional structures, public economics, property law, social movements and policy. Introductory research methods precede Public Economics, and the law gateway precedes its dependent courses.
alternatives.distinctness: Compared with the closest programme, this route replaces much of the earth-system, spatial-data and environmental-technology sequence with law, political institutions, diversity, communication, design and public decision-making. Ten courses differ, exceeding the 30-EC floor.
progression: Sociology, law and economics support later study of constitutional structures, public economics, property law, social movements and policy. Introductory research methods precede Public Economics, and the law gateway precedes its dependent courses.

alternatives.label: Global connections, migration and place
alternatives.concept: Studies how empires, trade, migration and political institutions shape places and identities. History, economics, sociology and cultural analysis offer different ways to investigate those connections.
alternatives.labelReason: Modern history, sociology and comparative politics support later work on empires, international economics, Indigenous histories, migration narratives, inequality and international law. General methods precede the final historical research paper.
alternatives.distinctness: This route replaces most planning, design and environmental-technology content with empire, international relations, global political economy, migration-related inequality, race, heritage and transnational histories. It differs by at least nine courses from each earlier alternative.
progression: Modern history, sociology and comparative politics support later work on empires, international economics, Indigenous histories, migration narratives, inequality and international law. General methods precede the final historical research paper.

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

core: Human geography and spatial planning: how people, institutions and environments shape places across scales
Urban development, housing, land use, collaborative planning and inclusive regional governance
Spatial, quantitative and qualitative research using GIS, statistics, interviews, fieldwork and independent inquiry
Globalisation, migration, economic and cultural geography, population change and regional inequality
Climate impacts, physical geography, landscapes and spatial-environmental sustainability
Place-based field research culminating in an independent bachelor project
adjacent: Urban governance, institutions and policy implementation
Migration, global connections and uneven regional development
Spatial sustainability through climate, water, environmental systems and landscape change
questions: How can cities and regions become more sustainable, inclusive and resilient?
How do institutions, economies, migration and social power shape spatial development and everyday life?
How can spatial data, mixed methods and field evidence support defensible planning decisions?

blocks: Both investigate how physical processes and human interventions shape landscapes. Living with Water focuses on water and adaptation in deltas.
Both study how institutions and stakeholders shape decisions. The UCR course focuses on sustainability policy.
Earth Observation uses GIS and satellite and drone data to study environmental change. Groningen’s GIS course builds a broader foundation in geographical analysis.
Both study physical processes that shape the Earth’s surface. Dynamic Earth focuses on geological processes and evidence.
Spatial Planning uses GIS and remote sensing for environmental problems. It covers a different part of planning from Groningen’s study of urban development, housing, land use and planning history.
UCR economics covers markets, policy and trade. The comparator studies the location of economic activity and regional differences.
Heritage, media and sociology offer related ways to study identity and culture. Groningen’s course centres geographical relationships between people and places.
UCR covers stakeholder decisions in sustainability governance and analysis of public policy. The Groningen course gives spatial planning processes dedicated attention.
Sociology offers a related perspective on people and institutions. The external course introduces geography and planning as disciplines.
Governance, policy, law and political economy
Both study European institutions and policymaking. The UCR course focuses on EU politics, while Groningen applies that context to geography and planning.
Earth science and delta courses include field or site inquiry. Groningen requires a separate geography fieldwork course abroad.
Spatial, quantitative, qualitative and research methods
Both develop quantitative research skills. Econometrics focuses on statistical inference for economic relationships.
Both introduce statistical analysis and data interpretation. UCR applies these methods to business and social-science questions.
Both develop research questions and use evidence. At UCR, teams investigate sustainability questions from a regional partner.
Both develop qualitative research design and interpretation. The UCR course applies them in small social research projects.
UCR courses address some social and historical aspects of population change. Groningen offers dedicated study of population geography.
Living with Water and the environmental courses address aspects of rural places and land use. They provide no single counterpart to rural geography.
Modern History and Life & Travel Writing address migration through history and personal narratives. Groningen studies migration patterns and their relation to development.
No selected course provides a dedicated study of ageing from a geographical perspective.
UCR’s introductory statistics and econometrics courses address related skills at different stages. Neither supplies a separate match for this course.
Social theory and research courses consider how evidence and interpretations are formed. The selections do not include a dedicated philosophy of social science course.
The selected UCR courses include research projects. The Groningen thesis is a separate degree requirement.
The 30 EC is open choice. The UCR courses shown belong to planned study schedules.

selection.assessment: The closest option combines environmental spatial planning, GIS, place-based inquiry and social analysis. Public policy and global connections add distinct directions with different advanced courses and research questions. All pass the four-course distinctness floor. The three-option limit is reached.

notes.text: UCR offers environmental spatial planning, GIS, social research and policy analysis. Groningen provides more sustained training in population and rural geography, housing and urban planning, and requires dedicated geographical fieldwork and a thesis.

audience.programmeDescription: Human Geography and Planning at the University of Groningen studies how people, economies and institutions shape places. Students use fieldwork, maps, statistics and interviews to investigate questions such as housing, migration and regional development.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The closest UCR option combines environmental planning, spatial data and social research. Two related options focus on public policy and on global connections.

componentNotes.y2-restricted-elective: Healthy Ageing is one example of the four options for this 5 EC requirement.
componentNotes.y3-choice: Students may choose electives, a minor, exchange or a supervised internship. Electives require approval and may include up to 10 EC of first-year courses.
componentNotes.y3-thesis: The thesis follows GIS, Statistics 2, Qualitative Research Methods and Quantitative Research Methods.
componentNotes.y3-fieldwork: Fieldwork Abroad requires at least 90 of the first 120 EC by September 1 of the academic year in which the student participates.
